content:
Three strands structure the present review: the comparative effects of direct corrections and metalinguistic codes, learner preferences across feedback forms, and the emerging role of automated feedback in revision.

Learners reported significantly lower mental effort when processing direct corrections targeting grammatical issues (Bonilla López et al., 2018). These findings suggest that feedback explicitness shapes cognitive engagement, though the design does not isolate whether processing ease translates into durable accuracy gains.

Direct correction combined with metalinguistic explanation was favoured most often (215/447 responses, 48.10%), ahead of direct correction alone (111/447, 24.83%) (Liu & Wu, 2019). Preferences also varied by proficiency: at the lower level, 7 of 8 students wanted feedback solely from teachers, whereas at the higher level, 5 of 6 preferred feedback from both teachers and peers (Liu & Wu, 2019). The evidence suggests that learner beliefs are proficiency-sensitive, though the non-randomised, single-programme design limits generalisability.

Automated writing evaluation (AWE) introduces a distinct revision dynamic. Zhang and Hyland (2018) documented contrasting engagement profiles: one learner resubmitted an essay 13 times and raised her score from 79 to 90, while another resubmitted once and spent under 14 minutes on the task. Teacher feedback addressed more error types (16) than AWE feedback (8), though assignment differences may have confounded this comparison (Zhang & Hyland, 2018). Students reported spending more time revising after AWE feedback (6.2 hours) than after peer (5.8) or teacher feedback (4.7), and 88% submitted more than five times (Zhang & Hyland, 2021). This case study's single-classroom scope limits generalisability (Zhang & Hyland, 2021).

EFL teachers largely marked all errors comprehensively, whereas ESL teachers tended toward selective feedback on frequent error types (Mao et al., 2024). That review is limited by its exclusion of peer and computational feedback and by possible publication bias (Mao et al., 2024). The present paper addresses this gap by examining how direct, metalinguistic, and automated feedback conditions differentially shape revision behaviour and engagement in L2 writing.

meta_evaluation_reasons.sentence: Across these strands, evidence is strongest for immediate revision effects and weakest for durable accuracy gains, and no supplied study isolates how feedback form, rather than feedback source, drives revision behaviour.

verifications.explanation: The claim's central proposition — that learners reported significantly lower mental effort when processing direct corrections targeting grammatical issues — is stated in the source. The abstract reports: "A mental-effort based measure of cognitive load revealed that learners’ cognitive load estimates proved significantly lower processing direct corrections targeting grammatical issues." Section 5.4 confirms the significant effect of condition on reported mental effort and that "the cognitive load imposed by revision after DCF+G was significantly lower than that after ME+GN (p < 0.001, SE = 0.350)", and the conclusion states "learners’ cognitive load estimates proved significantly lower when corrections were provided directly and they targeted grammatical issues only." The self-report nature of the measure is also supported ("Based on self-reporting"; "learners reported on their perceived amount of mental effort"). No assertion is contradicted and no peripheral assertion is absent, so the claim is verified.

The peripheral contrast is also stated: "In contrast, teachers working in ESL contexts were inclined to a more selective approach ... through which they paid special attention to several linguistic targets, such as the most frequent error types in student texts." Both propositions are supported, no contradiction exists, and no hedge is removed (the source's "largely" and "inclined to" are preserved in the claim's "largely" and "tended toward").

uncited_sentences.sentence: These findings suggest that feedback explicitness shapes cognitive engagement, though the design does not isolate whether processing ease translates into durable accuracy gains.
The evidence suggests that learner beliefs are proficiency-sensitive, though the non-randomised, single-programme design limits generalisability.

Across these strands, evidence is strongest for immediate revision effects and weakest for durable accuracy gains, and no supplied study isolates how feedback form, rather than feedback source, drives revision behaviour [NEEDS CITATION].
The present paper addresses this gap by examining how direct, metalinguistic, and automated feedback conditions differentially shape revision behaviour and engagement in L2 writing.
Research on written corrective feedback (WCF) in second-language (L2) writing converges on a central distinction between what feedback corrects and how learners act on it.

Three strands structure the present review: the comparative effects of direct corrections and metalinguistic codes, learner preferences across feedback forms, and the emerging role of automated feedback in revision.
Experimental work indicates that feedback form conditions both accuracy during revision and learners' processing experience.
Preferences do not align neatly with experimental effects.
Automated writing evaluation (AWE) introduces a distinct revision dynamic.
